About: the mean free path of a hard-sphere molecule in a gas

Source

Concept
Mean free path of a hard-sphere molecule (d = 0.37 nm, m = 28 u, T = 300 K) in an ideal gas with n = p/kBT and collision cross-section σ = πd².
Serves
Explaining the mean free path among molecules frozen in place and among moving molecules, and how it depends on pressure at fixed temperature.
Measurement
300 tagged molecules in a periodic 20 nm box; λ = D/N, total distance over total collisions since the last control change. The chart plots nσλ against N on fixed axes; the previous run stays in grey. The Readouts panel below the controls shows p, n, N, the measured λ and the current nσλ.
View
One tagged molecule's current flight, same scale on both axes; grey dots are centres within 3d of the flight axis, placed above or below by a perpendicular chosen at the flight's start.
Controls
Pressure 1.0–4.0 MPa; other molecules frozen or moving with Maxwell velocities. Each change restarts the count.
Inquiry
Five questions, each answered and then checked by running the gas and reading the chart and the λ readout, followed by a summary card.
Misconception
Probed through the answer choices; each choice has its own feedback, shown only after a choice is made.
Model
The 300 tagged molecules collide only with the untagged ones, elastically; the untagged molecules pass through one another. This leaves the Maxwell distribution and the collision count unchanged.

Pedagogy principles applied

Commit, then checkEach card gates Next on a committed choice; the answer is found by running the gas, never shown in advance.
Feedback per choiceEach of the four choices on a card has its own explanation of why it holds or fails.
Operational quantitiesλ is the measured D/N of 300 molecules; nσλ is plotted from the same numbers the Readouts panel shows.
Real values, honest scaleTrue size, mass and temperature; the flight is drawn at one scale in both directions; the time-lapse is stated in the view title.
Stable axesView fixed at −2 to 24 nm by ±3 nm; chart fixed at 0–4000 collisions by 0–1.5, so a change in the settled value is a real change.
Comparison on one scaleThe previous run stays as a grey trace on the same axes until the next control change.
Late revealEach reference level (1 for frozen, 1/√2 for moving) is added to the chart only after the question that asks the student to find it.
The Mean Free Path of a Molecule
Current flight of tagged molecule 1 · drawn to scale · 10 ps of gas time per 1 s at 1×
Measured mean free path nσλ against N

Guided Inquiry

1 · Frozen targets

Keep the other molecules frozen and the pressure at 2.0 MPa, press ▶ Play, and watch the chart until about 4000 collisions have been counted. Where does the chart settle, and what does the measured mean free path read?

2 · Halving the pressure

Keep the other molecules frozen, and lower the pressure from 2.0 MPa to 1.0 MPa, as if pumping half the gas out. What happens to the measured mean free path and to the chart?

3 · Letting the targets move

Return the pressure to 2.0 MPa and switch the other molecules to moving, leaving the tagged molecules with the same Maxwell distribution of speeds as before. Where does the chart settle now, and what does λ read?

4 · Where the struck molecule was

Keep the moving gas at 2.0 MPa, and watch a dozen or so finished flights, each held on screen with the thin grey track of the struck molecule. Where was the struck molecule when the flight began?

5 · Why the factor √2

Compare the two settled values at 2.0 MPa: in the moving gas the tagged molecule has about 1.41 times as many collisions per nanometre as in the frozen gas. Why is the factor √2 and not some other number?

6 · The mean free path

A molecule of diameter d strikes every centre within d of its path, so it sweeps a cylinder of cross-section σ = πd² and makes one collision per length 1/nσ.

When the other molecules move too, meetings come at the mean relative speed √2 v̄, so λ = 1/(√2 nσ): 3.4 nm for nitrogen at 2.0 MPa and 300 K.

At fixed temperature n = p/kBT, so λ goes as 1/p: at 1 atm the same gas has λ of about 70 nm, nearly 200 molecular diameters.

The Mean Free Path of a Molecule

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A molecule in a gas flies straight until it hits another one. This sim follows 300 tagged nitrogen molecules, counts every collision they have, and measures the mean free path λ: the distance flown per collision.

What you'll learn

  • What fixes the number of collisions per nanometre of path.
  • How λ depends on the gas density and so on the pressure.
  • What changes when the other molecules move instead of standing still.
One flight of a tagged molecule: from one collision to the next, past the other molecules.

What's on screen

  • Top plot: the current flight of tagged molecule 1, to scale, with the same scale on both axes. Grey dots are other molecules' centres within 3d of the flight axis; the dashed outline is the swept cylinder named in the key.
  • Bottom plot: nσλ against the number of collisions counted N. The bright line is this run, the grey line the previous one; labelled reference levels are added to the chart as you progress.
  • Readouts: p, n, N, the measured λ and nσλ.
See itPress Play at the opening settings and watch the counts build. Watch for: N counting up in the Readouts, a held flight with its length ℓ each time the tagged molecule collides, and the grey dots drifting past.

03

A molecule sweeps a cylinder of radius d and hits every centre in it

Model a molecule as a hard sphere of diameter d = 0.37 nm. Two such spheres touch when their centres are d apart, so a moving molecule collides with every molecule whose centre lies within d of the line its own centre travels along. It sweeps a cylinder of radius d, and the area of its cross-section is the collision cross-section (1.32).

Notes (1.32). Here σ = 0.430 nm2.

If the centres of the other molecules are scattered at random, n per unit volume, a length ℓ of the cylinder holds nσℓ of them. One collision therefore takes ℓ = 1/nσ, and that is λ when the others stand still. At 2.0 MPa, n = 4.83×1026 m−3, so λ = 4.82 nm and the chart of nσλ settles at 1.

The swept cylinder. The tagged molecule and a struck one touch when their centres are d apart.
See itKeep the other molecules frozen at 2.0 MPa and press Play; wait about 15 s for 4000 collisions. Watch for: the measured λ settling near 4.8 nm and the line of nσλ levelling near 1.
04

Halving the pressure doubles λ

At fixed temperature n = p/kBT, so the density is proportional to the pressure. The box holds 3863 molecules at 2.0 MPa and 1931 at 1.0 MPa, so n falls from 4.83 to 2.41×1026 m−3.

The cylinder is the same, since d has not changed, but it now holds half as many centres per nanometre. λ = 1/nσ therefore doubles, from 4.82 nm to 9.63 nm. The chart plots nσλ and not λ, so it settles at 1 again.

λ against p for frozen targets, 1/p. Dots mark the slider's steps.
See itFrozen targets, 1.0 MPa, press Play. Watch for: n halved on the Readouts at once, then λ settling near 9.6 nm with the chart near 1 again.
05

Moving targets give a shorter λ, by a factor √2

Whether two molecules meet depends on their motion relative to each other, so the speed in the collision rate is the mean relative speed vrel. The distance covered is still set by the tagged molecule’s own mean speed v. With vrel = √2 v (the next section), the tagged molecule makes √2 times as many collisions per nanometre.

Notes (1.34). τ is the mean time between collisions.

At 2.0 MPa, n is unchanged at 4.83×1026 m−3, but λ falls to 3.40 nm and the chart settles at 1/√2 = 0.707. The tagged molecule is not slowed: its mean speed stays 476 m/s.

nσλ against N from two runs of the sim at 2.0 MPa. Dashed: 1/√2.
See itReturn to 2.0 MPa, switch to moving targets and press Play. Watch for: n unchanged on the Readouts, λ settling near 3.4 nm and the chart near 0.71 instead of 1.
06

The factor √2 is the relative velocity

Write the pair’s kinetic energy with the centre-of-mass velocity V and the relative velocity vrel = v1 − v2. The energy then splits (1.33): ½mv1² + ½mv2² = ½(2m)V² + ½(½m)vrel².

The Boltzmann factor then splits into one factor for V and one for vrel, so the relative velocity is distributed exactly like the velocity of one molecule whose mass is ½m. A mean speed goes as 1/√m, so halving the mass multiplies it by √2: vrel = √2 v. For nitrogen at 300 K, v = 476 m/s and vrel = 674 m/s.

Maxwell speed distributions for one nitrogen molecule and for the relative velocity of two.

The tagged molecule still covers only v of path each second, while meetings arrive at vrel. That ratio is the √2.

07

The struck molecule usually began outside the cylinder

A moving target does not wait in the cylinder. A flight of mean length 3.4 nm takes about 7 ps, and in that time another molecule moves about 3.4 nm too, several diameters.

The cylinder that counts is the one swept in the target’s own frame, with a length set by the relative speed. In 300 finished flights of this sim at 2.0 MPa with moving targets, 90 per cent of the struck molecules began more than d from the axis, 2.9 nm away on average, about eight diameters. About 7 per cent began behind the tagged molecule.

One flight from the sim, drawn to scale. The struck molecule starts well outside the dashed cylinder.
See itMoving targets at 2.0 MPa, press Play and watch about a dozen flights. Watch for: after each flight the thin grey track of the struck molecule, starting several diameters off the dashed cylinder and crossing into the tagged molecule’s path.
08

Where it matters

  • Air at one atmosphere. The same formula (1.35) with the sim’s σ gives λ ≈ 67 nm at 300 K, about 182 molecular diameters. The sim’s box holds gas at 10 to 40 atmospheres, where λ is a few nanometres.
  • Pumping a vessel out. λ ∝ 1/p. Once λ exceeds the size of the container molecules cross it without meeting. The effusion condition, a hole small compared with λ, is easy to meet in a vacuum and hard at atmospheric pressure.
  • Real molecules. σ is best taken as a measured area, a few times the geometric one, so the sim’s hard-sphere numbers give the size of λ, not an exact value for a real gas.
  • Transport. The notes use λ next as the step length when molecules carry momentum, energy or their own number, which gives viscosity, thermal conduction and diffusion.
Notes (1.35): λ at fixed T goes as 1/p.
Go deeper: what the sim measures

The measured λ is the total distance flown by 300 tagged molecules divided by their total collisions, so at N = 4000 it still carries a scatter of a few per cent: runs of this sim read nσλ between about 0.97 and 1.03 for frozen targets and 0.68 to 0.74 for moving ones. Only collisions of tagged molecules, always with untagged ones, are counted, and the untagged ones pass through one another, which leaves the Maxwell distribution unchanged.

09

Summary

In one line. The mean free path is the distance a molecule flies per collision; this sim measures it directly and lets you test what it depends on.

Key points

  • A molecule sweeps a cylinder of radius d, so σ = πd² and, among frozen molecules, λ = 1/nσ.
  • With n = p/kBT, λ ∝ 1/p at fixed temperature.
  • Moving targets add √2 to the collision rate through vrel = √2 v, so λ = 1/(√2 nσ).

Common mix-ups

  • “The mean free path is the gap between neighbouring molecules.” At 2.0 MPa the spacing is about 1.27 nm; λ is 4.82 nm, nearly four spacings.
  • “The cylinder has radius d/2.” Centres touch at d. A radius d/2 would make σ four times too small and the chart settle near 4.
  • “Moving targets leave λ unchanged, since n is the same.” The relative speed is √2 v: λ = 3.40 nm.
  • “The tagged molecule slows down in a moving gas.” Its mean speed stays 476 m/s; the √2 is in vrel = 674 m/s.

Things to try on your own

  • Run frozen targets at 1.0, 2.0 and 4.0 MPa and check that λ times p stays the same.
  • Run moving targets at 4.0 MPa and compare λ with 1/(√2 nσ) = 1.70 nm.
  • Switch from frozen to moving mid-run and compare the grey line with the bright one.
